Duration, including travel between stops: eight hours.

Elevation: 2,800 m.

Average temperature: 20°C by day and 10°C at night.

On this sightseeing tour of Quito, take in the views of the city's historic churches, domes and rooftops and discover its colonial art and architecture, local legends and traditions.

Quito, Ecuador's capital, was founded in the 16th century on the ruins of an Inca city and stands at 2,800 m. Colonial architecture survives in the historic centre. Its buildings and richly decorated interiors showcase the Quito School, which brought together Spanish, Italian, Moorish, Flemish and Indigenous artistic traditions. Its artists carved stone and wood to depict major religious events. On a 90-minute walk through the Old Town, you'll see why the historic centre is on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

Quito takes its name from the Quitus people, who inhabited the region long before the Spanish conquest. The city had served as an Inca capital before Sebastián de Benalcázar took it in 1533. It was granted Spanish city status in 1541. Its full name is San Francisco de Quito, and it remained the capital of the Quito territory until the end of Spanish colonial rule.

The Franciscans were the first religious order to establish themselves in Quito. They immediately began building a monastery that became a centre of education and art, with schools of painting and sculpture.

Plaza Grande, the main square, is framed by the cathedral, Presidential Palace, Archbishop's Palace and City Hall. We'll also visit the Jesuit church, one of the city's finest examples of colonial art, with its intricately carved façade.

Next, visit the Basílica del Voto Nacional, or Basilica of the National Vow. The French architect who designed it took inspiration from Notre-Dame de Paris. The basilica is considered Ecuador's foremost example of neo-Gothic architecture and one of the most remarkable in Latin America. Founded in the 19th century, it is considered unfinished. Look for gargoyles and carvings of animals native to Ecuador and the region, including caimans, turtles, boobies and monkeys.

The basilica is 140 m long and 35 m wide, with a 30 m central nave. Its two front towers rise 115 m, making it one of the tallest buildings in Quito.

See the contrasts of the capital in its Old Town and newer districts. From the El Panecillo viewpoint, beside the winged statue of the Virgin Mary, the city's patron, you can look out over the whole city.

Then head to the equator, known here as the Middle of the World. We'll visit both sites associated with the equator line:

1. Ciudad Mitad del Mundo. This visitor complex, owned by the provincial government of Pichincha, is in San Antonio parish, north of central Quito. Its monument commemorates the 1736 geodetic expedition that placed the equator here. Built between 1979 and 1982, the 30 m monument marks the spot where the line was then believed to pass. A line running out from the centre of the monument represents the equator, and countless visitors have crossed it over the years. GPS measurements in the 20th century placed the actual equator 240 m north of the complex.

2. Intiñan Museum. Try activities the museum presents as equator demonstrations, such as watching water swirl, balancing a hen's egg and walking along the equator line. Learn about ancient cultures and the tsantsa ritual, and see totems from several South American cultures. The grounds also feature traditional dwellings from different cultures in Ecuador, including a house with objects once owned by an Indigenous family that lived there many generations ago.

Stops: Basilica of the National Vow, the main square, the Golden Church, Plaza de San Francisco, the hill with the Virgin Mary statue, the Intiñan Museum and Mitad del Mundo.

Return to your hotel. The evening is free.
